Market Makers, Investors & How Options Are Used

Who participates in the options market, why they trade, and how a market-making firm like Akuna Capital operates.

Who Uses the Options Market?

The options market has two distinct types of participants with very different goals. Understanding the difference is key to understanding how options are priced and traded.

🏦 Market Makers

Firms like Akuna Capital whose job is to create the market — always ready to buy or sell options to anyone who wants to trade.

  • They don't have a strong directional opinion on stocks
  • Profit mainly from the bid-ask spread
  • Execute the same trade thousands of times per day
  • Goal: stay risk-neutral (not bet on direction)
  • Manage imbalances between buyers and sellers

👤 Investors / Traders

Everyone else — retail traders, hedge funds, pension funds — who trade options for a specific reason.

  • Protection: hedge a stock portfolio
  • Income: collect premium by selling options
  • Speculation: bet on direction or volatility
The bid-ask spread is the gap between what the market maker will buy at (the bid) and sell at (the ask). For example: bid = $1.00, ask = $1.10. Each trade, the market maker earns $0.10. Do this 10,000 times a day and it adds up — even without having a view on where stocks are going.

Why Investors Use Options

There are three main use cases. Knowing why someone is trading an option helps you understand if the price is fair.

1. Protection (Hedging) — Buying Puts

Most people hold stocks through 401ks, IRAs, or direct investments. They're worried about a big market drop. Buying a put option gives them a floor — like insurance on their portfolio.

Protective Put Strategy

You own stock at price P. You buy a put with strike K. If the stock falls below K, your put gains value and offsets the loss. Above K, you keep all upside (minus the cost of the put premium).

Cost of put = $1. Below strike K you're protected; above K you profit with a slight drag from the premium paid.

2. Income Generation — Selling Options

If you own stock and think it won't move much, you can sell call options against it (called a "covered call"). You collect the premium upfront as income. The trade-off: if the stock rockets up past the strike, you don't fully participate.

Covered Call Strategy

You own stock + sell a call at strike K. The sold call caps your upside but you keep the premium (shown as the slight profit below the breakeven). If the stock falls, the premium provides a small buffer.

Covered call: own stock, sell call at K. Max profit = premium + (K − cost basis). Capped above K. Breakeven = stock cost − premium received.

Key insight: Option sellers collect premium today but take on risk. Option buyers pay premium today but gain protection or leverage. Market makers sit in the middle, trading both sides.

3. Speculation — Directional or Volatility Bets

Speculators use options when they have a view on where a stock is going — up, down, or sideways. Unlike buying stock outright, options let you express nuanced views:

  • Bullish: Buy calls (or sell puts)
  • Bearish: Buy puts (or sell calls)
  • Neutral / Low volatility: Sell options and collect premium
  • High volatility expected: Buy options (both calls and puts)

How Akuna Trades (Market Maker Perspective)

Akuna Capital is a market-making firm. Rather than betting on stock direction, Akuna:

  • Posts bids and offers on hundreds of options simultaneously
  • Collects the spread on each trade ("edge")
  • Stays risk-neutral by hedging away directional exposure
  • Manages a portfolio of options — tracking complex risk characteristics like the Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta)
Think of a market maker like a currency exchange booth at an airport. They buy euros at 1.08 and sell at 1.10, profiting on the spread. They don't care which direction the dollar moves — they just profit from being the intermediary. Options market makers do the same with option contracts.

Formal Option Definitions

A call option gives the holder the right — but not the obligation — to buy one unit of an underlying asset at strike price K on (European) or before (American) expiration date T. A put option gives the right to sell at K.

Type Exercise Formal Payoff
European CallOnly at Tmax(ST − K, 0) = (ST − K)⁺
European PutOnly at Tmax(K − ST, 0) = (K − ST)⁺
AmericanAny time ≤ TWorth ≥ European equivalent

Intrinsic value = payoff if exercised right now: (S − K)⁺ for calls, (K − S)⁺ for puts. Option price = Intrinsic Value + Time Value, and Time Value ≥ 0 always.

ITM / ATM / OTM — Defined
Term Meaning Call (K vs S) Put (K vs S)
ITM — In the Money Intrinsic value > 0 (profitable to exercise now) S > K S < K
ATM — At the Money Strike ≈ current stock price S ≈ K S ≈ K
OTM — Out of the Money No intrinsic value; only time value S < K S > K

Example: Stock at $45. The $42 call is ITM (S>K, intrinsic=$3). The $45 call is ATM. The $48 call is OTM (only time value).

Why is Delta highest for ITM and ~0 for deep OTM?
Delta = the probability (roughly) that the option expires in the money, adjusted for discounting. Think of it this way:
• Deep ITM call (e.g., $42 call, stock at $55): Almost certain to expire ITM. Every $1 the stock moves, the option gains ~$1. Delta ≈ 1.
• ATM call (e.g., $45 call, stock at $45): 50/50 chance of expiring ITM. Delta ≈ 0.5.
• Deep OTM call (e.g., $48 call, stock at $35): Very unlikely to expire ITM. The stock would have to move $13 — very rare. Delta ≈ 0.
More precisely in BSM: Δcall = e−qTN(d+), where N(d+) is the cumulative normal probability. d+ captures how far the stock is from the strike, adjusted for time and vol. Deep ITM → d+ is large → N(d+) → 1. Deep OTM → d+ is very negative → N(d+) → 0.

No-Arbitrage Price Bounds

These bounds require zero model assumptions — pure no-arbitrage logic. Violating any bound creates a money machine:

Lower call bound: C ≥ max(S − e−rτK, 0)
Upper call bound: C ≤ S
Lower put bound: P ≥ max(e−rτK − S, 0)
Upper put bound: P ≤ e−rτK

Intuition: A call can never be worth more than the stock itself. If C < S − e−rτK, buy the call, short the stock, invest Ke−rτ risk-free → guaranteed profit at T in every state.

Early Exercise: American Options

Option Early Exercise? Reason
American Call (no dividends)❌ Never optimalSelling the call dominates — you keep time value and interest on K
American Call (with dividends)⚠️ SometimesExercise just before ex-div date to capture the dividend
American Put⚠️ SometimesDeep ITM put: interest on K can exceed remaining time value; better to collect K now

Put-Call Parity — Formal

Two portfolios with identical payoffs must have identical prices (no-arbitrage). This gives us the exact relationship between call and put prices:

No dividends: C − P = S − e−rτK
Continuous dividend yield q: C − P = e−qτS − e−rτK
General: C − P = e−rτ(F − K)   where F is the forward price

Proof: Portfolio A (long call + cash e−rτK) and Portfolio B (long put + long stock) both pay max(ST, K) at T, so C + e−rτK = P + S.

💡 Market makers monitor put-call parity deviations live. Any deviation beyond the bid-ask spread is an arbitrage opportunity that gets closed almost instantly.

Monday Key Takeaways

  • Market Makers create liquidity and profit from bid-ask spreads — they want to be risk-neutral
  • Investors trade options for protection, income, or speculation
  • Buying a put is the most common hedging tool — it acts like portfolio insurance
  • Selling options generates income but creates risk if the market moves against you
  • Market makers like Akuna manage portfolios of options, tracking Greek risks across many positions
Tuesday · Sept 23

Volatility — The Heart of Options Pricing

Everything in options comes back to volatility. Today covers what it is, how it's measured, how option prices are calculated, and how it changes over time.

What Is Volatility?

Volatility measures how much a security's price moves around. A calm, boring stock has low volatility. A wild, unpredictable stock has high volatility.

Formal Definition

Volatility is the annualized standard deviation of daily percentage price changes. It tells you the typical magnitude of price swings, expressed as a yearly percentage.

It is one of the most critical inputs when pricing an option. More volatile underlying → options are worth more (more chance of ending in-the-money).

If a stock has 20% volatility, that means over the course of a year, the stock's price moves within a range of roughly ±20% with about 68% confidence. A stock with 60% volatility can swing much more — its options will be much more expensive.

Two Types of Volatility

📈 Historical Volatility (HV)

Calculated from past price data. You look at a set of past prices and compute the standard deviation of returns.

  • Backward-looking (what did happen)
  • Fully measurable and objective
  • Usually computed close-to-close
  • Can be calculated over different time windows (10-day, 30-day, etc.)

Example: 30-day HV of 13.3% means the stock moved about 13.3% annualized over the past 30 days.

🔮 Implied Volatility (IV)

Derived from current option prices in the market. Rather than calculating from history, you ask: "What volatility does today's option price imply?"

  • Forward-looking (what the market expects)
  • Changes continuously with option prices
  • The key number traders focus on
  • Can differ from historical vol — this gap is where edge lives

Example: If an option costs $2.00, you can "reverse-engineer" it to find IV = 16.0%. If the same option costs $2.50, IV = 18.3%.

Implied Volatility as a Price in Its Own Right

This is a crucial insight for market makers: Options are really just volatility contracts. When Akuna looks at an options chain, they don't see "$2.00 call" — they see "16% implied volatility." Trading options is really trading volatility.

Two Views of IV

View 1 (Input → Output): The option price is $2.00 → solve for the volatility implied by that price → IV = 16.0%.

View 2 (Output → Input): You believe vol will be 18%, so you calculate the "fair" option price using that vol → then compare to market to find if options are cheap or expensive.

Converting Volatility to Expected Price Moves

If you know the implied volatility, you can estimate how much the market expects the underlying to move over any time horizon.

Expected 1-Day 1-Standard-Deviation Move
σ_daily = IV / √252

Expected N-Day Move
σ_N = IV × √(N / 252)

Example: IV = 16%, Current Price = $50
σ_1day = 0.16 / √252 = 0.16 / 15.87 ≈ 1.0% → $0.50 move per day
σ_5day = 0.16 × √(5/252) ≈ 2.3% → ~$1.15 over 5 days
A 1-standard-deviation move means the market has a ~68% probability of staying within that range. If the 1-day σ is $0.50 on a $50 stock, there's about a 68% chance the stock doesn't move more than $0.50 in a single day. If you see a move bigger than that, it's an "above-average" day.

Why Lognormal Distributions?

You might wonder: why not just use a standard bell curve? Two reasons:

  • Stock prices can't go negative — a normal distribution allows for negative values
  • Percentage gains compound differently than percentage losses (a 50% drop requires a 100% gain to recover)

So option pricing models use a lognormal distribution instead, which only allows positive prices and correctly accounts for compounding effects. The upside tail is slightly longer; the downside is capped at zero.

The lognormal distribution is bounded at zero (stock prices can't go negative) and has a longer right tail — matching how stock returns actually compound over time.

Basic Option Pricing (Expected Value Approach)

At its core, an option's value is just the expected payoff at expiration, discounted to today. Here's a simplified version:

Example: 4-Outcome World

Suppose a stock can only end at 4 prices, each equally likely (25% probability):

OutcomeStock PriceProbabilityCall Payoff (K=100)Weighted Value
O1$5025%max($50−$100, 0) = $0$0.00
O2$10025%max($100−$100, 0) = $0$0.00
O3$15025%max($150−$100, 0) = $50$12.50
O4$20025%max($200−$100, 0) = $100$25.00
Call Option Value$37.50
General Formula for Option Value
Option Value = Σ [ P(outcome_i) × max(Price_i − Strike, 0) ]

The real-world version (Black-Scholes) does this with a continuous probability distribution (lognormal) instead of discrete outcomes.

The Black-Scholes Model

Black-Scholes is the industry-standard formula for pricing European options. It takes the expected-value approach above and applies it to a continuous lognormal distribution.

Inputs (What You Know)

  • S — Current stock/underlying price
  • K — Strike price
  • T — Time to expiration (in years)
  • r — Risk-free interest rate
  • σ (sigma) — Volatility (the big unknown!)

Output (What You Get)

The theoretical fair value of the option. Plug in all 5 inputs → get a price.

Or reverse it: plug in the market price → solve for σ → that's the Implied Volatility.

Black-Scholes Key Term (d1)
d1 = [ ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2) × T ] / (σ × √T)

This term captures how far the current price is from the strike, adjusted for time and volatility. A higher d1 means the call is more likely to finish in-the-money.
Don't memorize the full Black-Scholes formula. The key insight is: volatility (σ) is the ONLY unknown. Everything else (stock price, strike, time, rates) is observable. Since nobody knows future volatility, nobody knows the "true" fair price — which is why there's a market!

Volatility Term Structure

Here's something important: options with different expiration dates don't all have the same implied volatility. The graph of IV across different expiry months is called the volatility term structure.

  • Near-term options often have higher IV — events (earnings, Fed meetings) loom close
  • Longer-dated options often have lower IV — time smooths out individual shocks
  • The shape can be normal (front lower, back higher) or inverted (front higher during fear/crisis)

Inverted (purple): near-term IV spikes during crises (VIX > 40) and then calms for longer dates. Normal (green dashed): in calm markets, short-dated IV is lower and long-dated IV is slightly higher — the market expects more can happen over a year than a month.

The VIX and Market Fear

The VIX is often called the "fear index." It measures the implied volatility of S&P 500 options over the next 30 days. When markets are calm, VIX might be at 12–15. During crises (2008, Covid-2020), VIX spiked above 80.

Market-making insight: When volatility is high and markets are chaotic, bid-ask spreads widen. This is actually when market makers can earn the most — more uncertainty means wider spreads and more edge per trade. Akuna is designed to thrive in high-volatility environments.

Geometric Brownian Motion — The Stock Price Model

All modern option pricing starts with the assumption that stock prices follow Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM). The math is:

St = S0 · e(m − σ²/2)t + σBt

where Bt is standard Brownian motion (continuous-time random walk: independent increments, Bt − Bs ~ N(0, t−s)). Equivalently, using a standard normal ε:

St = S0 · e(m − σ²/2)t + εσ√t  ,   ε ~ N(0, 1)

Why GBM? Stock prices stay positive, log-returns are normally distributed, and percentage changes (not dollar changes) are i.i.d. — all consistent with empirical observations.

Lognormal Distribution — Properties & Worked Example

Since St is the exponential of a normal, it follows a lognormal distribution. Key formulas:

E[St] = emt · S0
StDev[St] = emt · S0 · √(eσ²t − 1)
95% CI: [S0e(m−σ²/2)t − 1.96σ√t,   S0e(m−σ²/2)t + 1.96σ√t]
Worked Example (IEMS 373): S0 = $100, m = 8%, σ = 20%, T = 1 year

E[S1] = e0.08 × 100 = $108.33
StDev[S1] = e0.08 × 100 × √(e0.04−1) = $21.88
95% CI = [S0e0.06−0.392, S0e0.06+0.392] = [$71.75, $157.15]
The 95% range spans almost $86 — stock prices are highly uncertain over 1 year!

Computing tail probabilities: Pr(St > K) = N(x) where:

x = [ln(S0/K) + (m − σ²/2)t] / (σ√t)

Example: for K=$110, x = −0.1766 → P(S > 110) = 42.99%. For K=$95, x = 0.5565 → P(S < 95) = 28.89%. So P(outside [95,110]) = 71.9%!

The Black-Scholes Formula — Complete

The BSM formula prices European options assuming the stock follows GBM. For a stock with continuous dividend yield q:

C = e−qT S0 · N(d+) − e−rT K · N(d−)
P = e−rT K · N(−d−) − e−qT S0 · N(−d+)

d− = [ln(S0/K) + (r − q − σ²/2)T] / (σ√T)
d+ = d− + σ√T

N(d−) = risk-neutral probability of call expiring ITM. N(d+) is the delta-adjusted version that accounts for how much of the option premium comes from that ITM scenario.

Deltas from BSM: Δcall = e−qTN(d+),   Δput = −e−qTN(−d+)

BSM Worked Example — ATM Straddle Pricing

Setup: S = K = $100, σ = 25%, r = q = 0, T = 1/12 (one month to expiry)

Since r = q = 0 and S = K → ln(S/K) = 0, so:
d− = −½ × σ × √T = −0.5 × 0.25 × √(1/12) = −0.0361
d+ = +0.0361
N(d+) = 0.5144  |  N(d−) = 0.4856

Call price: C = 100 × (0.5144 − 0.4856) = $2.88/share
Put price: P = C = $2.88 (by put-call parity when S=K, r=q=0)

Selling 10 straddles (each on 100 shares):
Total premium = ($2.88 + $2.88) × 100 × 10 = $5,760 collected

From Binomial to Black-Scholes

BSM isn't magic — it's the limiting case of the Binomial Tree model. In the binomial model, the stock can go up to uS or down to dS each period. The key insight: you can construct a replicating portfolio (Δ shares + borrowing B) that matches the option's payoff in both states:

Δ = (Cu − Cd) / [(u − d)S]   ← option delta
Option price C = ΔS − B   ← no-arbitrage

The risk-neutral probability p = (erΔt − d)/(u − d) prices the option as: C = e−rΔt[p·Cu + (1−p)·Cd]. The real-world probability of the stock going up never enters the formula. When the binomial tree uses u = eσ√Δt, d = e−σ√Δt, and N → ∞ periods, this converges exactly to the BSM formula.

Tuesday Key Takeaways

  • Volatility = annualized standard deviation of price changes. It's the most important input to any option price
  • Historical Vol = what happened in the past. Implied Vol = what the market expects going forward
  • Implied Vol is derived by reverse-engineering current option prices — it's the market's best guess at future volatility
  • Expected daily move = IV / √252. Expected N-day move = IV × √(N/252)
  • Options use lognormal distributions because stock prices can't go negative and gains compound
  • Black-Scholes turns the "expected payoff" idea into a continuous formula. The only true unknown is volatility
  • IV changes across different expiration months — this creates the volatility term structure
  • The VIX measures near-term implied vol of the S&P 500 — it's the market's "fear gauge"

Options Chains, Greeks & Market-Making Mechanics

How to read a real options chain, what the Greeks tell you about risk, and how market makers think about buying, selling, and capturing edge.

Reading an Options Chain

An options chain is a table listing all available options on a stock or index — every combination of strike price and expiration date. Each row is a different strike. Columns show the price (bid/ask) and risk measures (the Greeks).

Key Columns in an Options Chain

ColumnWhat It Means
StrikeThe price at which you can buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying
Bid / AskThe current market price range. Bid = what you can sell at. Ask = what you can buy at. The gap between them is the spread.
IV (Implied Vol)The volatility implied by this specific option's market price
Delta (Δ)How much the option price changes for a $1 move in the underlying
Gamma (Γ)How much Delta changes for a $1 move in the underlying
Vega (ν)How much the option price changes for a 1% change in implied volatility
Theta (Θ)How much value the option loses per day due to time decay
Think of the Greeks as dials on a dashboard. Delta tells you directional exposure (are you effectively long or short the stock?). Vega tells you vol exposure (do you benefit from increasing vol?). Theta tells you time exposure (are you losing money as each day passes?). Gamma tells you how fast your directional exposure is changing.

How Market Makers Use Vega to Set Widths

Market makers don't just set a fixed bid-ask spread for every option. They scale the spread based on vega — the option's sensitivity to volatility changes.

Vega-Based Width Formula

The width of a market maker's bid-ask spread is roughly proportional to vega:
Width ≈ Vega × volatility_uncertainty_factor

Example: If the 400-strike option has Vega = 0.229, and you're uncertain about vol by ~0.5 vol points, the minimum width on that option would be about 0.229 × 0.5 ≈ 0.11. Market quotes this option 0.13 wide.

Higher vega options need wider markets because small vol moves cause large price changes. Deep in-the-money options or very short-dated options may have lower vega, allowing tighter spreads.

How Market Makers Form Their Own "Theoretical Values"

Every market maker runs their own pricing model (essentially their own version of Black-Scholes) using their own implied volatility assumptions. This produces a "theo" — theoretical value — for each option.

What happens when two MMs disagree?

  1. MM1 thinks fair IV = 32%, prices call at $1.04
  2. MM2 thinks fair IV = 30%, prices call at $1.00
  3. MM2 sees MM1's offer at $1.04 — it looks expensive to MM2
  4. MM2 buys at $1.04, and now a trade happens
  5. Both adjust their theos and markets until they converge

When you disagree with the market

If you think the market has priced an option too cheap (its IV is below your estimate of true vol), you buy it. If you think it's overpriced, you sell it. The market moves until buyers and sellers agree on a price.

This is how price discovery works. Collective opinion of all market participants determines the price.

Edge vs. Variance — The Market-Maker Tradeoff

This is one of the most important concepts in market making. Every time you trade an option, you collect edge (your profit from the spread). But you also take on variance (uncertainty about where the option eventually ends up).

Edge

The expected profit per trade from buying at the bid or selling at the ask relative to theoretical fair value. Small but consistent. Example: collect $0.01 of edge on 2,000 trades = $2,000 in edge.

Variance

The uncertainty (potential loss) from holding an option position until expiry. If you sell a call at $1.06 (collecting $0.01 edge), but the stock moves massively and the call expires worth $50, you lose a lot despite collecting your edge.

Example from Lecture

A market maker sells options across many strikes. By having offsetting positions (some long, some short, across different strikes and expiries), the overall portfolio's risk is much smaller than any individual position.

  • Total edge collected across all trades: $2,044
  • Max expected loss from variance: small (because positions net out)
  • The goal is to collect edge reliably while keeping variance manageable through diversification and hedging
The game: Trade and collect small amounts of edge repeatedly. Use offsetting positions to keep overall risk small. Manage the portfolio so that even if individual options go against you, the portfolio stays healthy. This is the core of market making.

Hedging with Delta — Cash Omega

When a market maker buys or sells an option, they immediately take on delta risk — directional exposure to the underlying stock. To stay risk-neutral, they hedge this by buying or selling the underlying stock (or futures).

Delta Hedge Example
You sell 1 call option on 100 shares with Delta = 0.40
→ You are effectively short 0.40 × 100 = 40 shares of stock equivalent
→ To hedge: buy 40 shares of stock (or 40 deltas' worth of futures)
→ Now your net delta = 0. You're directionally neutral.

If the stock then moves $1, your option position changes by ~$40 in value,
but your stock hedge gains ~$40, netting out to ~$0.
Delta hedging is why market makers don't care which direction the stock goes. They continuously buy/sell shares to stay "flat delta." What they're really trading is volatility — not direction. If realized volatility ends up higher than the IV they sold, they lose. If lower, they profit.

Delta Hedging in Practice — BSM Worked Example

From BSM: Δcall = N(d+) and Δput = −N(d−). Here's a full numerical example of delta-hedging a short straddle:

Position: Short 10 straddles (each on 100 shares) with S=K=$100, σ=25%, r=q=0, T=1/12

Δcall = N(d+) = +0.5144 per share
Δput = −N(d−) = −0.4856 per share
Δlong straddle = 0.5144 − 0.4856 = +0.0288 ≈ 0 (ATM straddles are nearly delta-neutral!)

Position delta = −1,000 shares-equivalent (short 10 × 100 shares) × 0.0288 = −28.8 shares

To delta-hedge: Buy 29 shares of stock to neutralize directional exposure.
After hedging, the position is delta-neutral — P&L depends on realized vol vs. implied vol, not stock direction.

The gamma problem: As S moves, delta changes (that's gamma). The short straddle gains if the stock sits still (theta decay) but loses if the stock moves a lot (negative gamma). A market maker delta-hedging this position must re-hedge continuously as the stock moves.

Put-Call Parity in the Options Chain

Every row in the options chain should satisfy put-call parity: C − P = e−qτS − e−rτK. Any deviation beyond the bid-ask spread is an arbitrage. This means:

  • If you can price the call, you can back out the fair put price — and vice versa
  • Market makers use this to synthesize positions (e.g., synthetic long = long call + short put)
  • Violations show up in real data but are tiny (<$0.05) and rarely executable after transaction costs

Wednesday Key Takeaways

  • An options chain shows all strikes and expiries — each row has price, Greeks, and IV
  • Bid-ask width is proportional to vega — higher-vega options have wider markets
  • Market makers run their own pricing models with their own IV assumptions ("theos")
  • When MMs disagree on vol, trades happen — this is price discovery
  • Edge = the small profit per trade from the spread. Variance = the risk of large moves against you
  • Market makers manage large portfolios of offsetting positions to collect edge while minimizing net variance
  • Delta hedging removes directional exposure — MMs are really trading volatility, not stock direction
Thursday · Sept 25

The Volatility Curve — Smile, Skew & Surface

Why different strikes have different implied volatilities, what the vol smile/skew looks like, and how to think about vol across both strike and time in 3D.

The Big Question: Why Don't All Strikes Have the Same IV?

You might expect that all options on the same stock with the same expiry would have the same implied volatility. After all, they're all pricing the same underlying asset's moves. But they don't — and understanding why is crucial to professional options trading.

Imagine buying "hurricane insurance" for a house. Insurance for a Category 5 hurricane (extreme move) costs more per dollar of coverage than insurance for a minor storm (small move). The market prices extreme outcomes differently than average outcomes. Options do the same thing — downside strikes often carry higher implied vol than at-the-money strikes because markets tend to crash harder than they rally.

The Volatility Smile and Skew

When you plot implied volatility vs. strike price for a given expiry, you get a curve — not a flat line:

Volatility Skew: OTM puts carry higher IV (demand for downside protection), with a smaller elevated wing on the upside (tail risk fear).

Reminder: What OTM/ATM/ITM mean for calls and puts

For a call: OTM = stock price < strike (unlikely to be exercised). ATM = stock ≈ strike. ITM = stock > strike.

For a put: OTM = stock price > strike (unlikely to be exercised). ATM = stock ≈ strike. ITM = stock < strike.

Example with stock at $100: The $95 put is OTM (stock hasn't fallen to $95 yet). The $105 put is ITM (stock already below strike). The $100 call is ATM.

🙂 Volatility Smile

Both OTM puts AND OTM calls have higher IV than at-the-money options. "OTM puts" = low strikes (below current price); "OTM calls" = high strikes (above current price). The curve is U-shaped. Common in currency/commodity markets.

  • Symmetric: both tails are expensive
  • Reflects fear of large moves in either direction

📉 Volatility Skew (Smirk)

OTM puts (low strikes, below current price) have notably higher IV than OTM calls (high strikes, above current price). Asymmetric. Very common in equity markets.

  • Reflects fear of market crashes (stocks fall fast)
  • Investors buying low-strike puts for downside protection drives up their IV
  • The 2008 crash made this even more pronounced
Wait — can OTM puts be replaced with ITM calls?

Yes — and this is a key insight from put-call parity. Consider a $95 put when stock is at $100 (OTM put). By put-call parity: C − P = S − Ke−rT, so the $95 call and $95 put are mathematically linked. The $95 call is now ITM (stock at $100 > strike $95). Both the OTM $95 put and the ITM $95 call reflect the same underlying risk — but they attract different traders:

  • Portfolio managers buy the OTM put for crash protection (paying up for it → inflated put IV)
  • Traders using ITM calls for the same strike pay the exact same IV (parity enforces this)
  • So "high OTM put IV" and "high ITM call IV" are the same thing — just viewed from two sides of parity

In practice, traders often quote and observe the put side for low strikes (because that's where the demand is), but the call at the same strike carries identical implied vol. This is why market makers must maintain a consistent vol curve — applying one vol to both the call and put at each strike.

Why Does Skew Exist? Supply & Demand

Implied volatility at each strike reflects the balance of supply and demand for options at that strike. Let's be precise about what "OTM puts" and "OTM calls" mean here:

  • OTM puts = strike prices below the current stock price. Example: stock at $410, the $390 put is OTM. These are the "crash protection" strikes — you only profit if the stock falls sharply.
  • ATM options = strike near current price ($410 put or $410 call). Most liquid, most fairly priced.
  • OTM calls = strike prices above current stock price. Example: the $430 call is OTM. You only profit if the stock rallies above $430.
  • OTM puts: Huge demand from fund managers hedging portfolios → IV is bid up → expensive relative to ATM
  • ATM options: Most trading happens here → competitive pricing → "fair" IV
  • OTM calls: Some demand from investors writing covered calls, some from speculators → usually somewhat elevated but less than puts
Call IV vs. Put IV at the Same Strike — Are They Different?

This is a common point of confusion. For any given strike, the implied vol is the same for both the call and the put — because of put-call parity. If you price the $395 call at 22% IV, the $395 put must also be priced at 22% IV (otherwise there's a risk-free arbitrage).

So when we say "OTM puts have higher IV than OTM calls," we are not comparing the call and put at the same strike — we're comparing across different strikes:

  • The $390 put (OTM, low strike) might have 30% IV
  • The $410 put/call (ATM) might have 20% IV
  • The $430 call (OTM, high strike) might have 22% IV

The skew says: low-strike options (whether quoted as puts OR calls) carry higher IV than high-strike options. Dealers and traders typically quote the put on the downside (because that's where demand is) and the call on the upside — but the vol is the same via parity.

Key Insight: Skew is NOT just about mathematics — it reflects real-world behavior. Every financial crisis has been a crash (markets fall fast) rather than a melt-up. This asymmetry in realized outcomes drives persistent demand for downside puts, which keeps put IV elevated. The market has "learned" from history.

Controlling Your Theoretical Values ("Theos")

Market makers adjust their own models' implied volatility inputs to reflect their view of where vol should be. You can't just pick any vol and make money — eventually options expire and are worth either zero or intrinsic value. Your theos need to be grounded in reality.

Example: Adjusting Theos to Trade

Suppose a market is quoting: Bid = $1.00 / Ask = $1.06 (10 contracts on each side)

  • Akuna's model says fair value = $1.03
  • Akuna sells at $1.06 (above their theo → collecting $0.03 of edge)
  • Later, the market comes back in: Bid = $1.01 / Ask = $1.04
  • Akuna buys at $1.02 to flatten (paying $0.01 above theo)
  • Net result: sold $1.06, bought $1.02 → profit of $0.04

The Volatility Surface — Adding Time

We've talked about IV across strikes for one expiry. Now add the time dimension: every expiry month has its own vol curve. Together they form a 3D shape called the volatility surface.

Axes of the Vol Surface

  • X-axis: Strike price (or delta-equivalent)
  • Y-axis: Time to expiry
  • Z-axis: Implied Volatility (%)

Each point on this surface is the IV of one specific option (one strike × one expiry).

What the Surface Tells You

  • Skew by expiry: Near-term options often show steeper skew than long-dated ones (crash in next 2 weeks is "urgent," crash in 2 years less so)
  • Level shifts: The whole surface moving up = market expects higher vol in general (e.g., macro event upcoming)
  • Calendar spreads: If 1-month IV is much higher than 3-month IV at the same strike, you can sell the front and buy the back
  • Akuna monitors the entire surface to find relative mispricings between neighbors
What Does a "Bump" on the Surface Mean?

A bump is when one specific option's IV is noticeably higher or lower than nearby options — its neighbors on the strike axis or the time axis. Here's what different bumps mean and what traders do about them:

Type of BumpWhat It Looks LikeLikely CauseTrade Implication
Strike bump$410 call IV = 25%, but $405 and $415 calls both at 20%Unusual demand at that strike (maybe a large OI player, or earnings pin)Sell the $410, buy wings ($405+$415) → short the "hump"
Expiry bumpMarch 20% IV, April 25% IV, May 20% IVKnown event in April (earnings, Fed) priced into that expiry onlyCalendar spread: sell April vol, buy March/May vol
Wing collapseFar OTM calls show lower IV than expectedCovered call sellers flooding supply at those strikesBuy the cheap wing, hedge with ATM options
Surface inversionShort-dated IV > long-dated IV (inverted term structure)Immediate fear/crisis. Market expects calm to return over time.Buy long-dated vol (cheap), sell short-dated vol (expensive)

The key insight: bumps that can't be explained by a fundamental supply/demand story are likely mispricings. Bumps that have a clear story (event risk, structural demand) are real and not necessarily tradeable — you need to judge whether the bump is "fair."

Picture a hilly landscape (the surface). You're standing on it. Every point you step on is a different option's implied volatility. Market makers map this entire terrain and look for "bumps" — places where one option's IV is out of line with its neighbors. Those bumps are trading opportunities (buy cheap, sell expensive and let them converge). But not every bump is a mispricing — some bumps are real (event risk, structural demand). The skill is knowing the difference.

Options Are Related — Spread Trading

Because options on the same underlying are all derived from the same future price distribution, they are mathematically connected. This creates spread opportunities:

  • Vertical Spread: Buy one strike, sell another in the same expiry (bet on direction with limited risk)
  • Calendar Spread: Buy one expiry, sell another at the same strike (bet on term structure of vol)
  • Diagonal Spread: Different strike AND different expiry

Example: 390 vs 400 Call

If the 390 call and 400 call are both in February expiry, they're closely related. The 390 will have a higher delta (more in-the-money) and slightly different IV. If you believe the 390 is priced at a higher IV than it "should be" relative to the 400, you might sell the 390 and buy the 400 — profiting if they converge.

Strategy Payoff Diagrams & When to Use Each

These diagrams show P&L at expiry as a function of stock price. The dashed vertical line = strike K. The horizontal dashed line = break-even (P&L = 0).

① Long Call — Buy the right to buy

Position: Pay premium C upfront. Profit if ST > K + C.

When: Bullish with limited capital. You want big upside but only risk the premium. Never loses more than the premium paid.

Greek profile: Δ > 0, Γ > 0, Θ < 0, Vega > 0

Why? Δ>0: you profit if stock rises (positive directional exposure). Γ>0: as stock rises, delta increases — your upside accelerates (convexity). Θ<0: you paid premium upfront; every day the option decays, shrinking the time value you hold. Vega>0: higher implied vol means the market thinks bigger moves are possible, making your option worth more.

Breakeven: K + premium paid. Below K at expiry = full loss of premium.

② Long Put — Buy the right to sell

Position: Pay premium P upfront. Profit if ST < K − P.

When: Bearish or hedging. Protective put = insurance on a stock you own. Risk is limited to P paid.

Greek profile: Δ < 0, Γ > 0, Θ < 0, Vega > 0

Why? Δ<0: you profit when stock falls. Γ>0: as stock falls, your put's delta becomes more negative — downside accelerates (same convexity logic as call). Θ<0: same as long call — time value erodes daily. Vega>0: higher vol makes the put more valuable.

Breakeven: K − premium paid. Above K at expiry = full loss of premium.

③ Long Straddle — Bet on a BIG move either way

Position: Long call + Long put at same strike K. Pay C + P.

When: Expecting large move (earnings, Fed, macro event) but unsure of direction. Profit if S moves more than the premium paid in either direction.

Max loss: C + P (S stays at K). Breakevens: K ± (C+P).

Greek profile: Δ ≈ 0, Γ > 0 (love big moves), Θ < 0 (biggest time-decay risk), Vega > 0

Why? Δ≈0: the call's positive delta and put's negative delta cancel at ATM. Γ>0 (maximum): straddles have the MOST gamma — a move in either direction profits. Θ<0 (most negative): this is the direct cost of that gamma; ATM options near expiry decay fastest. Vega>0: you're long two options, so you're the most sensitive to vol changes — rising IV helps you.

Breakevens: K − (C+P) on the downside, K + (C+P) on the upside. Stock must move more than total premium to profit.

④ Short Straddle — Bet stock stays near K

Position: Short call + Short put at same K. Collect C + P.

When: Low-vol environment, stock expected to be quiet. Market makers do this when they think IV is too high.

Max profit: C + P. Max loss: unlimited. Dangerous in tail scenarios.

Greek profile: Δ ≈ 0, Γ < 0, Θ > 0 (collect theta!), Vega < 0

Why? Mirror of the long straddle. Γ<0: you've sold convexity — large moves hurt you. Θ>0: the flip side of gamma; you collect time decay every day the stock stays quiet. Vega<0: rising IV increases the value of options you're short — bad for you. This is the market maker's classic position: collect premium, pray for calm.

Max profit zone: K ± (C+P). If stock moves outside, losses are theoretically unlimited.

⑤ Bull Call Spread — Bullish, capped upside

Position: Long K1 call + Short K2 call (K1 < K2).

When: Moderately bullish. Reduces cost of a naked long call by giving up unlimited upside above K2.

Example: Buy $45C/$1.23, Sell $48C/$0.23 → Net $1.00 debit. Breakeven $46. Max profit $2.00. Max loss $1.00.

⑥ Bear Put Spread — Bearish, capped downside

Position: Long K1 put + Short K2 put (K1 > K2).

When: Moderately bearish. Reduces cost of naked long put by giving up profit below K2.

Example: Buy $44P/$1.13, Sell $42P/$0.50 → Net $0.63 debit. Breakeven $43.37. Max profit $1.37. Max loss $0.63.

⑦ Short Strangle — Wide premium collection

Position: Short OTM call KC + Short OTM put KP. Collect premium, wider zone than straddle.

When: Expecting low realized vol but want more buffer than a straddle. Unlimited max loss.

Example: Sell $46C/$0.84 + $44P/$1.13. Receive $1.97. Zone: [$42.03, $47.97].

⑧ Iron Condor — Defined risk strangle

Position: Short strangle + Long wings further OTM. Capped loss, reduced premium.

When: You want strangle P&L but need defined max loss (for position sizing, risk management).

Example: Add $48C/$0.33 + $42P/$0.50 wings → Net $1.14. Max loss $0.86 vs unlimited for strangle.

⑨ Butterfly — Precision pin bet

Position: Long K1 call + Short 2 K2 calls + Long K3 call (equidistant strikes).

When: You strongly believe stock will expire near K2. Very cheap, very specific.

Use case: Pin risk around weekly/monthly options expiry (stocks often get "pinned" to high-OI strikes).

Buying vs. Selling — The Direction Distinction

A common source of confusion: short call and long put both profit when the stock falls — but they are fundamentally different. The diagrams below show the P&L shape of all four basic positions. K = strike price, B/E = breakeven, C = call premium, P = put premium.

① Long Call — Bullish
Pay C. Profit if S > K+C. Loss capped at C.
② Long Put — Bearish
Pay P. Profit if S < K−P. Loss capped at P.
③ Short Call — Neutral/Bearish
Collect C. Profit if S < K+C. Loss unlimited above.
④ Short Put — Neutral/Bullish
Collect P. Profit if S > K−P. Loss grows as S→0.

Key: ━━ Strike K   ╌╌ Breakeven   ━━ Zero P&L line

Position Direction view Risk Reward Key Greek Why use it?
Long CallBullishPremium paid (limited)UnlimitedΔ +, Γ +Leverage without unlimited downside
Short CallNeutral/BearishUnlimitedPremium received (limited)Δ −, Θ +Income generation, covered call
Long PutBearishPremium paid (limited)Up to K (S→0)Δ −, Γ +Hedging, bearish speculation
Short PutNeutral/BullishUp to K (S→0)Premium received (limited)Δ +, Θ +Income when bullish; sell insurance
💡 Key insight: Long options cost money upfront but cap your risk. Short options collect money upfront but create open-ended risk. A long put and a short call both profit when the stock falls, but the long put buyer chose to pay for that view (limited risk), while the short call seller is being paid to take on that exposure (unlimited risk).

Thursday Key Takeaways

  • Not all strikes have the same IV — the vol curve (smile/skew) reflects supply/demand for each strike
  • Equity markets typically show a skew (put wing higher than call wing) due to demand for downside protection
  • Skew exists because markets tend to crash harder than they rally — history is baked into option prices
  • Market makers actively manage their "theo" vol curve, adjusting it to trade profitably across many strikes
  • The volatility surface is a 3D map of IV across both strikes and expiry dates simultaneously
  • Options on the same underlying are interconnected — mispricings between related options create spread trade opportunities
  • Akuna tracks the entire surface across many products, allowing them to spot inconsistencies and trade them

Technology — FPGAs, Automation & Data-Driven Trading

How Akuna Capital uses hardware engineering, automated systems, and data analysis to execute faster and smarter than the competition.

Why Speed Matters in Market Making

Market making is a highly competitive business. When a good trade opportunity appears — say, an option offered below its theoretical value — multiple market makers see it at the same time. The fastest one wins. Speed is a genuine competitive advantage.

Winner-take-all dynamic: If you're 1 microsecond faster than your competitor in responding to a market quote, you get the trade and they don't. Over millions of trades, this speed advantage translates into millions of dollars of additional edge collected.

FPGAs — Hardware Faster than Software

Standard trading programs run on CPUs — software instructions processed sequentially. Akuna goes a step further and uses FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays), which are programmable chips that implement logic directly in hardware.

🖥️ Software (CPU) Approach

  • General-purpose processor
  • Instructions executed one by one
  • A simple trading decision function: ~202 instructions across 16 loops
  • On a 2.6 GHz machine: takes ~66 nanoseconds
  • Flexible and easy to update

⚡ FPGA (Hardware) Approach

  • Custom logic baked directly into the chip
  • Many operations execute in parallel, simultaneously
  • Same calculation: single-digit nanoseconds
  • Often 10–100x faster than equivalent software
  • Requires specialized engineering to design and program
Think of software like a single chef cooking each dish one at a time. An FPGA is like having 100 specialized chefs — one just for sauces, one for grilling, one for plating — all working simultaneously. The result comes out much faster because everything happens in parallel.

How FPGAs Work — Boolean Logic

FPGAs implement logic using basic Boolean algebra operations wired directly into the chip:

Three Fundamental Operations
AND gate: f = a AND b → output is 1 only if BOTH a=1 AND b=1
OR gate: f = a OR b → output is 1 if EITHER a=1 OR b=1
NOT gate: f = NOT a → output is the opposite of a

These three operations, combined, can represent ANY computational logic.
Combining many gates creates a "half-adder," "full-adder," comparators, etc.

Akuna designs these gate circuits to implement specific trading decisions — checking if a price is below a threshold, computing a sum, comparing two values — all in hardware rather than software.

The Full Trade Decision Pipeline

Here's how a trade decision flows through Akuna's system, in real time:

End-to-End Example

  1. Exchange sends a market update: "Call option offered at $0.50"
  2. Akuna's system has pre-calculated: Theo = $0.65, Offset = $0.05
  3. Decision rule: If offer ≤ $0.60 (= theo − offset), send a buy order
  4. $0.50 < $0.60 → BUY IT!
  5. With FPGA: this entire pipeline completes in single-digit nanoseconds
  6. With software: same decision takes ~66+ nanoseconds
The offset ($0.05): This is the minimum edge required to trade. Akuna won't buy at $0.64 even though that's below theo — they need at least $0.05 of edge to justify the trade and cover transaction costs and variance.

Automated Response Systems

Akuna runs many automated systems simultaneously that respond to market events in real time:

  • Auto-quoting: Automatically adjust bids and offers as the market moves
  • Auto-hedging: When a trade fills, automatically send the delta hedge order
  • Auto-theo adjustment: When a trade occurs, update theoretical values to reflect new information
  • Auto-risk checks: Monitor position sizes and halt trading if limits are hit

Automation Lifecycle

1. Akuna quotes a set of option prices
2. A trade occurs (someone buys Akuna's offer)
3. System automatically updates theos (you've revealed information about where vol should be)
4. System sends a delta hedge in the underlying
5. Markets re-quote automatically at new levels
6. Traders review performance data and refine the automation rules

Human role: Traders at Akuna don't manually click to trade every time. Instead, they spend their time monitoring automated systems, analyzing data to improve the automations, and making high-level decisions about risk limits and model parameters.

Data-Driven Decision Making

One of Akuna's core principles is making decisions based on data, not intuition alone. They capture enormous amounts of market data every single day.

📊 Historical Data Analysis

Use past data to improve future trading:

  • Identify patterns: "Every time we trade >X quantity on a single ticket, we lose money"
  • Adjust rules: reduce size thresholds, be more aggressive in hedging
  • Backtest new strategies: simulate on historical data before live trading
  • Terabytes of tick-by-tick data captured — every single market update

📡 Real-Time Dashboards

Monitor live trading for immediate course corrections:

  • "We've been winning consistently in the last 20 minutes — hold course"
  • "Our delta is drifting — hedge more aggressively"
  • Track fills, edge collected, Greeks exposure in real time
  • Compare actual vs. expected performance
Think of it like a GPS navigation system. You set your destination (target: collect edge, minimize variance). Real-time dashboards tell you where you are right now (live P&L, current Greeks). Historical data helps you improve the map (which roads to avoid, what shortcuts work). The automation is the car's engine doing the actual work — you steer at a high level.

Friday Key Takeaways

  • Speed is a genuine competitive advantage in market making — milliseconds and nanoseconds matter
  • FPGAs implement trading logic directly in hardware, running many operations in parallel — often 10–100x faster than software
  • FPGAs use Boolean logic (AND, OR, NOT gates) to build complex decision circuits
  • The full pipeline: receive market update → compare to theo → check offset → send order, all in nanoseconds
  • Automation handles quoting, hedging, and theo updates — traders focus on high-level oversight and improvement
  • Data-driven decisions: terabytes of tick data captured, historical analysis used to improve automation rules
  • Real-time dashboards allow immediate course corrections during the trading day

The Greeks — A Beginner's Glossary

Plain-language definitions of each Greek, what it measures, and how traders use it in practice.

The "Greeks" are sensitivity measures — each one tells you how much an option's price changes when one specific input changes. Think of them as the speedometer, fuel gauge, and temperature dial on an options dashboard.

🔵 Delta (Δ) — Directional Exposure

What It MeasuresChange in option price per $1 change in the underlying stock
Range0 to +1 for calls, −1 to 0 for puts
ExampleDelta = 0.40 → if stock rises $1, your call gains $0.40
At-the-moneyDelta ≈ 0.50 (50/50 chance of expiring ITM)
In-the-moneyDelta approaches 1.0 (moves almost like owning stock)
Out-of-the-moneyDelta approaches 0 (unlikely to expire in the money)
How MMs Use ItHedge delta immediately by buying/selling the underlying. Goal: keep portfolio delta near zero (direction-neutral)

🟢 Gamma (Γ) — Rate of Change of Delta

What It MeasuresHow much Delta changes per $1 move in the underlying
AnalogyIf Delta is your speed, Gamma is your acceleration
ExampleDelta = 0.40, Gamma = 0.05 → if stock rises $1, delta becomes 0.45
Highest WhenOptions are at-the-money and close to expiry (delta changes rapidly)
Long GammaYou benefit from large moves in either direction (you bought the option)
Short GammaYou lose from large moves (you sold the option)
How MMs Use ItLong gamma lets you collect profits by re-hedging as the stock moves. Short gamma requires constant re-hedging that costs money if stock moves a lot.

🟡 Vega (ν) — Volatility Exposure

What It MeasuresChange in option price per 1% (1 vol point) change in implied volatility
ExampleVega = 0.229 → if IV rises 1%, option gains $0.229 in value
Long VegaYou benefit from rising IV (you bought the option)
Short VegaYou lose if IV rises (you sold the option)
Highest WhenOptions have long time to expiry and are near-the-money
How MMs Use ItPrimary driver of bid-ask width. Higher vega = wider spread needed to compensate for vol uncertainty. Also used to compare options across different strikes (vol prices, not dollar prices).

🔴 Theta (Θ) — Time Decay

What It MeasuresHow much option value is lost per day, all else equal
ExampleTheta = −0.05 → option loses $0.05 of value per day
For BuyersTheta is negative — time passing hurts you (your option decays toward zero)
For SellersTheta is positive — time passing helps you (you keep collecting decay)
AcceleratesTheta decay speeds up as expiry approaches — most decay happens in the final weeks
How MMs Use ItShort options positions collect theta daily. Long gamma positions "pay" theta. The Gamma/Theta tradeoff is fundamental: you pay theta to own gamma (potential to profit from big moves).

🟣 Rho (ρ) — Interest Rate Sensitivity

What It MeasuresChange in option price per 1% change in interest rates
ExampleRho = 0.10 → if rates rise 1%, call option gains $0.10
MagnitudeUsually the smallest Greek in practice (interest rate changes are small and slow)
How MMs Use ItGenerally not a primary concern for short-dated options, but matters for longer-dated options (LEAPS) especially in changing rate environments

Greeks — Mathematical Definitions

Every Greek is a partial derivative of the option price C (or P) with respect to a market input. This is why they change continuously as markets move.

Greek Formula BSM Value (call) What moves it
Delta Δ ∂C/∂S e−qT N(d+) Moves toward 1 as S↑ (deeper ITM). Ranges (0,1) for calls, (−1,0) for puts.
Gamma Γ ∂²C/∂S² = ∂Δ/∂S e−qT N'(d+) / (S σ√T) Highest at-the-money near expiry. Same for calls and puts (put-call parity). Always ≥ 0 for long options.
Vega ν ∂C/∂σ S e−qT N'(d+) √T Highest ATM, grows with time to expiry (long-dated options are very vol-sensitive). Always ≥ 0 for long options.
Theta Θ −∂C/∂T − [S e−qT N'(d+) σ] / (2√T) − rKe−rTN(d−) Usually negative for long options (time decay). Accelerates near expiry (especially for ATM). Positive for short options.
Rho ρ ∂C/∂r KTe−rT N(d−) Positive for calls (higher rates → cheaper to hold stock → call worth more). Negative for puts. Usually the smallest Greek in practice.

Where N'(x) = e−x²/2/√(2π) is the standard normal PDF (not CDF).

Greeks Relationship Flowchart

The Gamma-Theta relationship is the most important one for market makers: Γ and Θ always have opposite signs for a given position. Here's exactly why — it's a mathematical inevitability baked into the BSM model itself.

The BSM PDE — the equation every option price must satisfy:
Θ + rS·Δ + ½σ²S²·Γ = r·C

Rearranged: Θ = r·C − rS·Δ − ½σ²S²·Γ

The term ½σ²S²·Γ is always the dominant driver near expiry. Because σ, S, and σ²S² are all positive:
• If Γ > 0 (long gamma) → that term is positive → Θ must become more negative.
• If Γ < 0 (short gamma) → that term is negative → Θ must become more positive.

Intuitively: gamma measures convexity (how much you gain from large moves). The BSM model says that convexity isn't free — you pay for it through time decay. A long straddle near expiry has maximum gamma (the payoff kink at K is most sensitive) AND maximum negative theta (it decays fastest). ATM options near expiry are the clearest illustration — their gamma spikes and their theta spikes simultaneously, always in opposite directions.

→ The bigger the move you could profit from, the faster you're losing value to time.

The Gamma-Theta Tradeoff — The Core Dilemma

This relationship is perhaps the most important concept for understanding options risk in practice:

Gamma vs. Theta — You Can't Have Both

Being long gamma (bought options) means you benefit when the market makes large moves — you can re-hedge at a profit. But you pay for this with negative theta — each day that passes without a big move, your options decay.

Being short gamma (sold options) means you collect positive theta every day — the clock works in your favor. But you're exposed to large moves — if the market crashes or rallies sharply, you lose.

You're always betting: "Will realized volatility be higher or lower than the implied vol I traded at?"

PositionGammaThetaWins WhenLoses When
Bought call/put+ Long− Negative (cost)Market moves a lotMarket sits still, time passes
Sold call/put− Short+ Positive (income)Market sits stillMarket moves sharply

Quick Reference: All Greeks at a Glance

GreekInput It MeasuresLong Option EffectShort Option Effect
Delta (Δ)$1 move in underlying+ (call) / − (put)− (call) / + (put)
Gamma (Γ)$1 move → change in delta+ (always positive)− (always negative)
Vega (ν)1% rise in implied vol+ (benefits)− (hurts)
Theta (Θ)1 day passing− (hurts, decays)+ (benefits, collects)
Rho (ρ)1% rise in interest rates+ (call) / − (put)− (call) / + (put)
You don't need to memorize exact formulas for any of these. The key is understanding what each one represents conceptually. When a trader says "I'm long gamma, short vega," it means they benefit from large price moves but are hurt by rising implied vol — so they'd want a market that moves but stays "within expected range."

Real SPY Options Data — Course Concepts in Practice

Everything taught Mon–Thu, shown with a real week of SPY end-of-day options data. ~23,000 rows, 320 strikes, 36 expiries.

📊 About This Dataset

This analysis uses end-of-day snapshots of SPY (S&P 500 ETF) options for the week of August 1–5, 2022. Each row represents one option contract (one strike × one expiry), recorded at market close. The data includes all the Greeks, implied vol, bid/ask, and volume for both calls and puts.

StatValueWhat It Means
Total rows22,962Individual option contracts observed
Strikes320From $85 to $720
Expiry dates36Options spanning 0 to 872 DTE

The Analyst's Chain of Thought — How We Decided What to Plot

Before writing a single line of plotting code, a good analyst works through a structured reasoning process. Here's exactly how to think about this kind of dataset — and why each plot was chosen in the order it was.

Phase 1 — Data Inventory: "What do I actually have?"

Before any analysis, read df.head(), df.dtypes, and df.describe(). You're asking three questions:

  • What are the dimensions? 22,962 rows × 29 columns. Each row is one (quote_date × strike × expiry) combo — a single option contract snapshot. So this is an options chain, not a time series of one stock.
  • What columns do I have? Greeks for calls and puts (Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta, Rho), implied vol for both sides, bid/ask/last/volume, DTE, strike distance. This is essentially a live Wednesday options chain captured at end-of-day.
  • What are the data types? Immediately spotted problems: C_IV, C_VOLUME, C_BID, C_ASK stored as strings (with whitespace). C_SIZE is a composite "10x50" format that needs parsing. These must be fixed before any calculation.

Phase 2 — Data Quality: "What needs cleaning before I can trust it?"

Always validate before plotting. With financial data, bad values produce misleading charts that can look plausible.

  • Strip whitespace on all string columns — column names had leading/trailing spaces ([C_IV] vs C_IV)
  • Cast types — convert string IV and volume columns to numeric with errors='coerce' (bad strings become NaN, not crashes)
  • Parse composite columns — split "10x50" bid-ask size strings into two separate integer columns
  • Handle impossible values — negative implied volatility is mathematically impossible (IV is a standard deviation, always ≥ 0). Set to NaN. This was a real data quality issue in the SPY dataset.
  • Check null patterns — 32% of call volume and 31% of put volume are null. Is this random? No — it's concentrated in far OTM strikes where nobody trades. That finding itself is informative: it tells you liquidity drops off sharply away from ATM, a concept covered in the Wednesday market-making mechanics section.

Phase 3 — Question Formulation: "What questions can this data answer?"

Now that you know your columns, map each one to a question worth asking. This is where theoretical knowledge from the course pays off — you know what to look for.

The market prices crash risk asymmetrically.IV skew exists → protective puts are expensive → tail risk is priced. Market makers must adjust theos by strike. Thursday — Vol Skew

Phase 4 — Plot Prioritization: "What order do we build in, and why?"

You can't plot everything at once. Prioritize by theoretical fundamentality and complexity — start with 2D cross-sections before building to 3D. A good sequence:

  1. Vol skew (2D: IV vs Strike, fixed expiry) — The single most important structural property of an options market. If you only have time for one plot, this is it. It tells you whether the market prices tail risk asymmetrically. → Chart 1
  2. Term structure (2D: ATM IV vs DTE) — The second dimension of volatility. Once you know the skew at one expiry, you want to know if the level of vol is consistent across time. → Chart 2
  3. Volume heatmap (2D: Strike × Expiry) — Sanity check: are the options we're analyzing actually traded? This validates whether the IVs we computed are from real price discovery or stale/illiquid quotes. → Chart 3
  4. Put-call parity (validation: residuals by strike) — Mathematical check on internal consistency. If parity breaks down, either the data is wrong or there's a structural explanation. Always good to run before trusting the data further. → Chart 4
  5. Daily IV movement (time series: ATM IV over dates) — Now that the static picture is understood, add the time dimension. How did vol move this week? Was there an event? → Chart 5
  6. 3D vol surface (3D: IV × Strike × DTE) — The synthesis. Only makes sense after you understand the 2D slices individually. This is the full picture that a market maker maintains in their model. → Chart 6
The meta-lesson: Every plot choice is driven by a theoretical question rooted in what you know about how options markets work. Data exploration without domain knowledge produces pretty charts. Data exploration with domain knowledge — from the course — produces insights. The order of charts above mirrors the order concepts were taught: Monday (market structure) → Tuesday (vol theory) → Wednesday (chains and liquidity) → Thursday (skew and surface).

Chart 1 — The Volatility Skew Tuesday Thursday

Why this chart first? Why fixed expiry?

The vol skew is the most fundamental structural property of an options market. Before anything else, you want to know: does this market price risk symmetrically or asymmetrically across strikes?

Why fix the expiry first? Implied vol changes across both strikes AND time. If you mix different expiries in one plot, you conflate two effects. By holding expiry constant (e.g., "look only at options expiring in 14 days"), you isolate the strike dimension — which tells you about skew and supply/demand for protection at specific levels. Once you understand the shape at one expiry, then you vary time (Chart 2). Always control one variable at a time.

Why near-term expiry? Near-term options (14–30 DTE) have the most trading activity, tightest bid-ask spreads, and most reliable IV estimates. Far-OTM strikes on long-dated options often have very little volume, making their IV noisy. Start with where the data is cleanest.

This is the vol skew from Tuesday's lecture, shown with real SPY data. The near-term expiry (around 14 DTE) plotted against strike price.

What You're Seeing

The steep left wing: OTM put strikes (below spot ~$410) carry significantly higher IV than ATM or OTM calls. This is the equity skew — the market permanently prices downside tail risk (covered in depth on Thursday). Demand for portfolio protection inflates put IV above the "fair" lognormal level.

The noisy right wing (above ~$425): These OTM calls are thinly traded. Wide bid-ask spreads cause the mid-price to be less reliable, leading to erratic IV values. This is the liquidity effect Akuna cited when setting wider markets on low-vega OTM options.

Akuna connection: A market maker seeing this would price OTM puts on a higher vol assumption than ATM options — their theo vol curve (the "vol smile input") accounts for this skew. Quoting a flat vol across all strikes would leave them badly mispriced on the wings.

Chart 2 — Volatility Term Structure Tuesday

Why ATM IV specifically? Why not all strikes?

To study how vol changes across time (the term structure), you need to hold the strike dimension constant, just as you held the time dimension constant in Chart 1. The cleanest way to do this is to always track the at-the-money (ATM) strike — the strike closest to the current stock price.

Why ATM specifically? ATM options are the most liquid (tightest spreads → most accurate IV), have the highest vega (most sensitive to vol changes → largest IV signal), and sit at the "center" of the vol surface where the skew effect is minimal — so you're measuring the level of vol, not the skew. Using a fixed dollar strike (e.g., always the $410 strike) would be wrong because as the stock moves, your fixed strike might drift from ATM to OTM, mixing the skew effect into your term structure measurement.

What the term structure tells you: If near-term and long-term IV are similar, the market is calm with no known catalysts. If near-term IV is much higher (inverted structure), the market is pricing in an imminent event — earnings, Fed announcement, macro data. If long-term is much higher (normal steep structure), the market expects conditions to get more uncertain over time.

ATM implied vol plotted against days to expiry (DTE) — the term structure of volatility discussed on Tuesday.

What You're Seeing

The term structure here is relatively flat with a slight upward slope at longer maturities. This contrasts with the inverted term structure (front month much higher) you'd see during a crisis like Covid — see the Tuesday VIX discussion. In August 2022 there were no major scheduled market-moving events that week, so short-dated and long-dated vol were similar.

The slight dip at very short DTE (near-zero days) and the gradual rise toward 12–18 months suggests the market expects mean reversion toward a slightly higher long-run volatility level — a core property of the vol term structure — essentially saying "things are calm now, but over a year or two, more things can happen."

Akuna connection: This flat-ish term structure means calendar spreads (same strike, different expiry) wouldn't be as obviously profitable as during a vol spike. Market makers monitoring the term structure would note the relative flatness and trade accordingly.

Chart 3 — Volume Heatmap: Where Is the Market's Attention? Wednesday

Total options volume (calls + puts) mapped across strikes and expiry dates. Darker = more activity.

What You're Seeing

Volume is heavily concentrated in near-term expiries (left side of chart) at strikes close to the spot price (~$410). Activity drops sharply beyond 2–3 weeks out. This tells us:

  • Most traders are expressing short-term views (income sellers, hedgers, speculators)
  • Longer-dated options (LEAPs) are much less liquid — wider spreads, less efficient pricing (see Wednesday on vega-based widths)
  • The market is "nearsighted": it cares most about the next 2–3 weeks
The median call volume was 0 and median put volume was just 2. Most contracts barely trade. Only ATM near-term options have deep liquidity. This is why bid-ask spreads on far-OTM or long-dated options are so wide — there's nobody on the other side to keep prices honest.

Chart 4 — Put-Call Parity: Is the Market Efficient? Monday Wednesday

Put-call parity is a fundamental no-arbitrage relationship (introduced in Wednesday's pricing section): C − P = S − K. Any deviation is a potential free lunch (arbitrage). Here we measure those deviations for 7–30 DTE options.

Put-Call Parity Relationship
C − P = S − K (simplified, ignoring rates and dividends)

Full form: C − P = S − K × e^(−rT) − PV(dividends)

Deviation = (C_last − P_last) − (S − K)
Near zero means the market is correctly pricing the relationship.
What You're Seeing

Deviations are small near ATM (spot ~$410), confirming the market is efficient in that region. The slight tilt — negative residuals below spot, positive above — is explained by the simplified formula not accounting for the risk-free rate discount on the strike and expected dividends. SPY pays dividends, which shifts the parity relationship. This is not an arbitrage; it's a known structural adjustment.

Akuna connection: Market makers enforce put-call parity. If a large deviation appeared, they'd immediately trade to capture the arb. Their speed advantage (FPGA tech from Friday) ensures they get there first.

Chart 5 — Daily ATM IV Movement: A Week in the Life Tuesday

ATM implied vol tracked day-by-day (Mon Aug 1 → Fri Aug 5) for the nearest liquid expiry. This shows how market sentiment evolved intra-week.

What You're Seeing

IV peaked mid-week and declined by Friday. One likely explanation: the first week of August coincides with major monthly economic reports (jobs report, PMI, etc.). Traders bid up IV at the start of the week in anticipation of these releases. Once the data came out and removed uncertainty, IV dropped. This is a classic pattern:

  • IV rises heading into known events (earnings, Fed meetings, NFP jobs report)
  • IV collapses immediately after the event — the uncertainty is resolved
  • Options traders call this "selling the event" — selling options before the event and buying them back after at lower IV. This is a direct application of the implied vol vs. realized vol gap concept from Tuesday.
The IV crush: This mid-week peak and end-of-week decline is a real-world example of the "IV crush" phenomenon. If you bought options going into that event expecting a big move, and the move happened but was smaller than IV implied, you likely still lost money as IV collapsed. The market "over-priced" the event.

Chart 6 — The 3D Volatility Surface Thursday Tuesday

The full volatility surface — IV plotted across both strike (X) and time to expiry (Y) simultaneously, for SPY calls.

What You're Seeing

The most striking feature is the steep "wall" in the low-strike / short-DTE corner. Near-term OTM puts carry extremely high IV. As DTE increases, the surface flattens — the skew effect diminishes for longer-dated options. This makes intuitive sense: over a longer horizon, a "crash" is less likely in the next 2 weeks vs. the next 2 months, so the urgency to buy downside protection is lower, compressing that premium.

The surface is the map that Akuna's pricing models must replicate and maintain — this is exactly the 3D vol surface from Thursday's lecture, now shown with real data. Every point is a separate option with its own supply/demand dynamics. Keeping this surface internally consistent — and spotting when a single point goes out of line — is where market-making edge is found.

Akuna connection: When Akuna sees a "bump" on the surface (one option's IV out of line with its neighbors), they have a clear trade: buy the low-IV neighbor, sell the high-IV bump, wait for convergence. Their models continuously scan the entire surface looking for exactly this. Thursday's lecture on "offsetting positions keeping overall variance low" is this principle in action — and the Wednesday edge vs. variance framework explains why it matters.

Real Data — Key Takeaways

  • The vol skew is real and steep on SPY: OTM puts consistently carry 5–15% higher IV than ATM options
  • The term structure was flat in Aug 2022 — a "calm" market environment, no major event risk driving near-term vol up
  • Volume is overwhelmingly concentrated in near-term ATM options — most of the market is short-sighted
  • Put-call parity holds very well near ATM, confirming efficient markets and active arbitrage enforcement
  • IV peaked mid-week, likely driven by monthly economic reports — a real example of "event IV" and the IV crush
  • The 3D vol surface confirms the theory: steep skew wall at low-strike/short-DTE, flattening over time
  • Every chart connects back to a concept from the course: each one is not just data — it's the market pricing something real
