Round 2 Practice — Strategy

  • Do P1, P6, P10, P14 first — these are the most likely to appear and cover the core patterns
  • Always state your approach before coding: "I'll use a hashmap here because I need O(1) lookups…"
  • Know your time/space complexity for every solution — they will ask
  • For the "complete the trading book" question: read the existing code's variable names carefully. They tell you exactly what's expected.
  • If you get stuck: brute force first, then optimize. A working O(n²) beats a broken O(n).
  • Practice writing solutions without an IDE — use paper or a plain text editor to simulate interview conditions

⑧ Completing Partial Functions — Round 2 Strategy

Step 1: Read the function name + docstring — the intent is always clear. Step 2: Identify the pattern (dict accumulation? sliding window? sort + scan?). Step 3: Write simplest correct solution. Then handle edge cases: empty list, single element.

# Example: complete net_delta()
def net_delta(trades, deltas_by_strike):
    """
    trades: [{"strike": K, "qty": Q, "side": "buy"/"sell"}]
    deltas_by_strike: {K: delta_value}
    Returns total portfolio delta.
    """
    total = 0
    for trade in trades:
        signed_qty = trade["qty"] if trade["side"] == "buy" else -trade["qty"]
        delta = deltas_by_strike.get(trade["strike"], 0)
        total += signed_qty * delta
    return total
⏭ Round 3 — Probability & Options Pricing (click to expand)

Round 3 — Probability & Options Pricing

This is where most candidates get cut. You need to be comfortable with expected value, basic probability, and intuitive options pricing — not Black-Scholes formula memorization, but conceptual understanding.

Probability questions — expect these types

Q: You flip a fair coin. If heads you win $3, if tails you lose $1. What's the expected value? Would you play?

Answer
EV = 0.5 × $3 + 0.5 × (−$1) = $1.50 − $0.50 = +$1.00 Yes — positive EV, always play a +EV game when the bet size is reasonable relative to your bankroll. This is exactly how market makers think: collect small positive EV thousands of times a day.

Q: A stock is at $100. It can go up $10 or down $10 with equal probability. What is a fair price for a call option with strike $100?

Answer — Expected Value Approach
Outcome 1: stock = $110 → call payoff = max(110−100, 0) = $10 (prob 50%) Outcome 2: stock = $90 → call payoff = max(90−100, 0) = $0 (prob 50%) Fair value = 0.5 × $10 + 0.5 × $0 = $5.00 Follow-up they may ask: "What if the stock could go up $20 or down $5?" → EV = 0.5 × $20 + 0.5 × $0 = $10. Higher volatility = more expensive call. ✓
Key insight to state: "This is the core of options pricing — an option is worth the probability-weighted average of its possible payoffs. Black-Scholes is just the continuous version of this same calculation."

Q: You roll a die. If it lands 6, you win $10. Otherwise you pay $X. What's the max X you'd pay to play?

Answer
EV = (1/6) × $10 + (5/6) × (−X) = 0 → (1/6) × 10 = (5/6) × X → X = 10/5 = $2.00 You'd pay up to $2.00 to break even. Less than $2 is a good bet. This is a "fair price" calculation — identical logic to pricing an option.

Q: Stock has 20% IV. What's the expected 1-day move? (mental math version)

Answer — the "16 rule"
√252 ≈ 16 (memorize this!) Daily move = Annual Vol / 16 = 20% / 16 = 1.25% per day For a $400 stock: 1.25% × $400 = $5 expected daily move (1 std dev) They may ask: weekly move? Weekly = Annual Vol / 16 × √5 ≈ Annual Vol / 7.1 = 20% / 7.1 ≈ 2.8% per week → $11.20 on a $400 stock
The "16 rule" is a standard trading floor shortcut. √252 ≈ 16. Divide annual vol by 16 to get daily expected move. Every options trader knows this.
⏭ Rounds 4 & 5 — Greeks, Hedging & Strategy Deep Dive (click to expand)

Rounds 4 & 5 — The Greeks Under the Hood

The confirmed question from Glassdoor: "How do options Greeks behave if the underlying moves up or down?" This is the core of the final rounds. Here's a complete model answer.

⭐ THE Question: "How do the Greeks behave when the underlying moves up or down?"

Walk through each Greek systematically. The interviewer wants to see you understand the relationships, not just recite definitions.

Delta (Δ) — moves with the underlying

Underlying moves...Call DeltaPut DeltaWhy
Up ↑Increases → toward +1.0Increases → toward 0Call goes deeper ITM; put goes further OTM
Down ↓Decreases → toward 0Decreases → toward −1.0Call goes OTM; put goes deeper ITM
Example
ATM call: Delta = 0.50. Stock rises $10 → call goes ITM → Delta = 0.70 ATM call: Delta = 0.50. Stock falls $10 → call goes OTM → Delta = 0.30 → This change in delta IS gamma (see below)

Gamma (Γ) — peaks at ATM, shrinks away from it

Underlying moves...Gamma of the optionWhy
Up ↑ (option goes deeper ITM)DecreasesDeep ITM options already move 1:1 with stock — delta can't increase much more
Down ↓ (option goes further OTM)DecreasesDeep OTM options barely move regardless of stock moves — delta stays near 0
Stays near ATMHighest / stays highATM is the "inflection point" where delta changes fastest
Key insight to state: "Gamma is highest ATM and near expiry — this is when delta is changing fastest. A large underlying move in either direction will reduce gamma on that specific option because it moves away from ATM."

Vega (ν) — driven by vol, but strike distance matters

Underlying moves...Vega of the optionWhy
Away from strike (either direction)DecreasesOTM options have lower vega — less chance of expiring ITM means vol matters less to their value
Stays ATMHighestATM options benefit most from vol increases — a big move in either direction helps them
Important nuance: the underlying moving doesn't directly change implied vol (vega is a sensitivity TO vol, not driven by price movement). But when the underlying moves, a different strike is now "ATM" — and that strike's vega is now highest. The vega of your specific option decreases as it goes OTM or deep ITM.

Theta (Θ) — time decay, affected by moneyness

Underlying moves...Theta of the optionWhy
Away from strike (OTM or deep ITM)Theta becomes less negative (less decay)OTM options have less time value to decay. Deep ITM options are mostly intrinsic value.
Stays ATMMost negative theta (decays fastest)ATM options have maximum time value — they have the most to lose from time passing

Pulling it all together — the model answer structure

How to frame your answer in the interview
"When the underlying moves up, for a call option: 1. Delta increases — the option becomes more sensitive to further moves (it's deeper in the money, moves more like the stock itself) 2. Gamma decreases — delta was changing fastest at ATM; as we move ITM, delta is already high and has less room to grow 3. Vega decreases — the option is now deeper ITM; vol matters less because it's already worth a lot based on intrinsic value 4. Theta becomes less negative — less time value remains to decay since the option has moved from ATM toward ITM For a put moving up: delta moves toward 0 (becomes less negative), gamma decreases, vega decreases, theta less negative — symmetric logic."

Other Greeks questions likely to come up

Q: If you're short gamma, what happens when the stock moves a lot?

Being short gamma means you've sold options. When the stock makes a large move, your delta changes rapidly — requiring constant, expensive re-hedging. Each time you re-hedge you're buying high or selling low (you have to chase the market). You lose money proportional to how much the stock moved (realized variance). This is why short-gamma traders hate volatility — and why they collect theta to compensate for that risk.

Q: You sell an ATM straddle (sell both a call and a put at the same strike). When do you make money? Lose money?

Answer
Selling a straddle = short both call and put ATM. You collect the combined premium upfront. Make money: stock stays near the strike at expiry. Both options expire worthless (or nearly so). You keep the premium. Lose money: stock moves significantly in either direction. The winning option (call if up, put if down) becomes worth more than the premium you collected. Breakevens: Strike ± total premium collected Example: Strike $100, collect $5 total → profit if stock stays $95–$105
Connect to Greeks: "A short straddle is short vega (you lose if IV rises), short gamma (you lose on large moves), and long theta (you collect daily decay)."

Q: What is delta hedging? Walk me through a real example.

Delta hedging removes the directional bet from an options position so you're only exposed to volatility, time, etc. Here's a concrete example:

Example
You sell 10 call contracts (1,000 shares) with delta = 0.40. Net delta = −0.40 × 1,000 = −400 (you're effectively short 400 shares) To hedge: BUY 400 shares of stock. Net delta = 0. You're directionally neutral. Next day: stock rises $5. Call delta increases to 0.50. Your hedge is now short: −0.50 × 1,000 + 400 = −100 shares net. You need to BUY 100 more shares to re-hedge. This re-hedging when the stock rises (buying) and falls (selling) is called "gamma scalping." If realized vol > IV you sold, you make more from gamma scalping than you paid in premium → profit.

Behavioral Questions — Resume-Based Answers

From Glassdoor: "Why Maven? Why trading? Things like this." Every answer should be rooted in your actual experiences, not generic scripts. Use the below as starting frameworks — adapt with your own words.

Resume Walk-Through (30-second version)

"I'm a junior at Northwestern studying Industrial Engineering and Economics. The most relevant project I've done is the IEMS 373 options project I led — we built a long strangle thesis on FedEx using implied volatility and premium analysis to select strikes, then refined the selection with Black-Scholes and breakeven logic. We also used LSTM-driven price and volatility forecasts to stress-test our assumptions. That project made options theory very concrete for me. Outside of that, I've worked on Markov regime-switching models applied to VIX for my honors thesis, and earlier built a gradient-based calibration pipeline in PyTorch that achieved a 64x accuracy improvement on an epidemic model. So I sit at the intersection of quantitative modeling and real data — which is what I understand Maven does."

Why Maven specifically?

"The IEMS 373 project made clear to me that options pricing is fundamentally about modeling uncertainty — we had to decide how much vol to embed in our strikes, and whether the market was mispricing tail risk in FedEx. The judgment call about when to trust the model and when to override it is exactly what I understand Maven analysts do. The JD says 'markets generate questions faster than anyone can answer them' — that resonates: in the options project, we generated six distinct analytical questions from one dataset (skew, term structure, volume concentration, parity, daily IV, surface). I want to be in an environment where that kind of rigorous-but-fast analysis has a direct trading outcome."

Why trading (not pure research or consulting)?

"I've done pure research and consulting — I enjoyed the rigor, but what I found missing was the feedback loop. In trading, you find out fast whether your thesis was right. My time leading an artillery squad in the Korean Army reinforced that for me: you make a decision with incomplete information, commit, and learn the outcome quickly. I also noticed that in consulting at Monitor Deloitte, the insights I produced were many steps removed from any actual decision. I want to be closer to the decision. Maven's analyst role — where analysis 'directly shapes trading decisions from day one' — is exactly the structure I'm looking for."

Tell me about the FedEx strangle (IEMS 373 project)

"As team leader, we built a long strangle thesis on FedEx. The thesis had two legs: first, we found macro catalysts — supply chain dynamics and shipping demand data — that we believed could cause a large move in either direction. Second, we used implied volatility analysis and premium data to assess whether the options were priced fairly for that uncertainty. We then used Black-Scholes to price the specific strikes we were considering and back-calculated the breakeven thresholds — how much the stock had to move for us to profit. We also applied LSTM-driven forecasts to stress-test the vol assumptions. The decision to go long the strangle rather than take a directional position was deliberate — we were confident in the uncertainty but not the direction."

Leadership / pressure story (Korean Army)

"I led a 4-person artillery squad for 18 months, managing classified geospatial data and firing accuracy calculations where errors had real consequences. I authored a 50+ page tactical manual and ran 2-month onboarding cycles for new members. Two things from that experience apply directly to trading: first, rigorous process documentation is risk management — the manual wasn't bureaucracy, it was how we ensured accuracy under time pressure. Second, making fast decisions with incomplete information and then being accountable for the outcome is a skill you can develop. That's what I did in the army and what I want to do in markets."

OA talking points (your SPY analysis)

  • Vol skew: "I observed a steep left skew — OTM puts had significantly higher IV than OTM calls. That's crash insurance demand. A market maker would need to adjust theoretical values by strike, not use a flat vol surface."
  • Put-call parity: "I checked put-call parity across all strikes. Deviations were small and within the bid-ask spread — the market is efficient. A few far-OTM outliers were likely stale quotes."
  • Volume concentration: "Volume concentrated in near-term ATM contracts. Median DTE for high-volume strikes was ~14 days. Far-OTM prices should be treated carefully — thin liquidity = noisy prices."
  • Mid-week IV spike: "ATM IV peaked mid-week then compressed by Friday — classic vol crush after a macro event. This is exactly why traders sell straddles before known events and close after."

Using Your OA Work in Later Rounds

The data exploration you did (the SPY options notebook) is directly relevant to what Maven described. Here's how to reference it in later rounds when asked about your analytical approach:

Things you found that are worth mentioning

I interpreted this as structural demand for downside protection from equity holders, not a pure model mispricing." → Shows you understand supply/demand drivers of options prices, not just math.

Interview Prep — Final Checklist

  • ✅ Round 1 OA done. Know what you found and be ready to discuss your methodology and insights.
  • 📌 Round 2 Python: Practice list loops, dict manipulation, and "fill in the missing function" style problems. Know pandas basics (groupby, pivot_table, merge).
  • 📌 Round 3 Probability: Be fluent in expected value, the "16 rule" for daily moves, and option pricing via EV. Speak in trader intuition, not just formulas.
  • 📌 Rounds 4–5 Greeks: Know exactly how Delta, Gamma, Vega, and Theta behave as the underlying moves up and down. Know the gamma-theta tradeoff cold. Practice explaining the delta hedging example out loud.
  • 📌 Behavioral: Prepare a genuine "Why Maven / Why trading" answer. Use JD language. Reference the OA work as evidence of your interest, not just your skills.
  • 📌 Your edge: You've done the options 201 course AND built real analysis on SPY options data. Most candidates haven't done either. Lead with what you've actually studied and found.
